chunks.source: Wikipedia — Washingtonia filifera var. robusta (Mexican fan palm)
chunks.text: The Mexican fan palm — treated by Plants of the World Online as a variety of Washingtonia filifera (var. robusta) though many horticultural and regional sources still call it the separate species Washingtonia robusta — is a tall, single-trunked fan palm in the Arecaceae, native only to a narrow range on the Baja California peninsula and in palm-oasis canyons of Sonora, Mexico, within the Sonoran Desert, yet it has become 'one of the most widely cultivated subtropical palms in the world'. It typically reaches about 25 m and occasionally up to 30 m, with large fan-shaped (palmate) leaves up to a metre across on spiny petioles, a tall inflorescence up to 3 m bearing many small pale orange-pink flowers, and small blue-black, thin-fleshed but edible fruit. A defining and much-discussed trait is that its older dead fronds are not shed on their own; left untrimmed they hang down and accumulate into a dense, skirt-like 'beard' that can run most of the trunk's length — a feature the article compares ecologically to a coral reef, since the dead-frond skirt in its native habitat becomes a micro-habitat for wasps, rodents, scorpions, birds and spiders, though in cultivated urban settings this same skirt is usually seen as a fire and pest hazard and is deliberately trimmed off ('skinning'), work that is dangerous enough that public-health authorities in California have issued specific arborist safety training for it. Prized for its very rapid growth, tall dramatic silhouette and tolerance of poor soils and urban pollution, it has been planted as an avenue and street tree across California, Arizona and the US Gulf Coast, the Mediterranean, the Middle East (street plantings are recorded in Israel and Turkey) and other subtropical regions worldwide, though the Wikipedia article notes only that it is 'naturalized' in these regions without detailing ecological impact — other sources (e.g. Cal-IPC) separately flag it as invasive in riparian areas in parts of its introduced range. It is comparatively cold-tender (hardy only to about -8°C) compared with its close, slower-growing, more cold-hardy relative Washingtonia filifera var. filifera (the California fan palm), and field research in Baja California suggests individual trees may live for over 500 years.

chunks.source: Cal-IPC (California Invasive Plant Council) — Washingtonia robusta
chunks.text: This invasive-species assessment is a useful counterweight to purely horticultural descriptions of the Mexican fan palm: while the species is beloved as a fast-growing, statuesque ornamental and street tree across warm, dry, subtropical regions (it is an extremely common sight lining boulevards in Los Angeles and similar cities, and by extension in comparable warm Indian cities where ornamental palm avenues are popular, though India-specific documentation is thin in the sources found here), Cal-IPC's listing exists precisely because the same qualities that make it a popular landscape choice — fast growth, prolific seed production carried by birds, and tolerance of varied soils — have allowed it to escape cultivation and establish in riparian corridors, canyon washes and other wild and semi-wild landscapes outside its tiny native range in Baja California and Sonora, where it can crowd out native vegetation along watercourses. This is a worthwhile caution for any park or civic planting programme considering the species purely as an attractive, low-maintenance 'palm tree' statement piece: its ornamental appeal and its potential to spread beyond where it is planted are two separate properties that should be weighed together, particularly near natural waterways.
